site.lab_name: Synthetic Biology and BioProcess Engineering Lab
site.home_intro: The Synthetic Biology and Bioprocess Engineering Lab at Kyung Hee University (KHU) engineers microorganisms into cell factories for sustainable biomanufacturing. Our work runs along three connected lines. First, we build the foundational tools that make non-conventional hosts — methylotrophic yeasts, oleaginous microalgae, marine protists, and methanotrophs — as tractable as model organisms, developing CRISPR/Cas9 multiplex editing, in vivo DNA assembly, and safe-harbor expression systems. Second, we apply metabolic engineering to convert renewable carbon — CO<sub>2</sub>, methane, methanol, and lignocellulosic sugars — into three families of products: industrial chemicals and fuels (white biotechnology), pharmaceuticals and nutraceuticals (red biotechnology), and food and feed materials (green biotechnology). Third, we are building an AI-driven, automated design–build–test–learn platform, so that strain development becomes a data-driven and increasingly self-directed process rather than a manual one. Together these efforts aim at bioprocesses that are not only environmentally sound but economically competitive.

research.overview_sub:
Sustainable Synthetic Biology and BioProcess Engineering
for the Production of Value-added Products
research.intro: Fossil-fuel dependence and continuous greenhouse gas emission have made sustainable routes to fuels, chemicals, and materials an urgent research priority. Our answer is the microbial cell: given the right genetic tools and the right process, microorganisms can convert CO<sub>2</sub>, methane, methanol, and inedible biomass into products that are today made from petroleum. We organize this work into three research lines — the foundational tools that make new hosts engineerable, the metabolic engineering that turns them into producers of chemical, pharmaceutical, and food materials, and the automation and artificial intelligence that shorten the design cycle for both.

topics.title: Development of foundational synthetic biology tools for diverse microorganisms
topics.body: Synthetic biology begins with the ability to modify an organism at will, and for most industrially attractive microorganisms that ability is still limited. We build the foundational toolkit that makes non-conventional hosts as tractable as the established model organisms: CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing and multiplex integration, modular cloning and in vivo DNA assembly, safe-harbor loci identified from transcriptional hotspots, RNAi-based knockdown, and transcription-factor engineering. Screening is treated as part of the toolkit rather than an afterthought, so that improved strains are obtained by selection from large populations instead of one at a time. We develop these tools across methylotrophic yeasts, oleaginous microalgae, marine protists, acid-tolerant yeasts, and methanotrophs, and our aim in each case is the same: to turn a promising but intractable organism into a well-characterised chassis that others can build on.

topics.title: Metabolic engineering for white, red, and green bioproducts
topics.body: With the tools in hand, the question becomes what to make. We redirect carbon flux in engineered strains toward three families of products, following the colour convention of industrial biotechnology. White — industrial chemicals, fuels, and materials, including organic acids, fatty acids and their derivatives, and bioplastic precursors. Red — pharmaceuticals and nutraceuticals, including long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids, carotenoids, and terpenoids. Green — food and feed materials, including microalgal biomass, single-cell protein, food-grade lipids, and natural pigments. The feedstocks are renewable and largely non-food — CO2, methane, methanol, and lignocellulosic sugars — and the same host organisms serve all three families; what differs is the pathway we install and the process we design around it. Pathway design, cofactor and redox balancing, tolerance engineering, and fermentation development are treated as one problem rather than as separate stages, because a strain that performs well only in a shake flask is not yet a useful result.
topics.hint: feedstocks → hosts → white / red / green products

topics.title: AI-driven automation: biofoundry and the self-driving lab
topics.body: Strain engineering is still largely manual, and the design–build–test–learn cycle remains the rate-limiting step in biomanufacturing. We are building an automated, data-driven platform to shorten it: standardised genetic parts and assembly protocols that a liquid handler can execute, high-throughput cultivation and analytics that generate consistent phenotype data, and machine-learning models trained on that data to propose the next round of designs. Combined with genome-scale metabolic models and techno-economic analysis, the aim is a biofoundry in which the choice of the next experiment is made from data rather than intuition — a step toward a self-driving laboratory for microbial cell factory development.
